column2: DE BesAR regime mis-dated: EEG 2012 tranche ladder applied from 2012, but it first binds benefit year 2013 — 2010–12 is the EEG 2009 Selbstbehalt regime
column3: TRIGGER: the DE MEDIUM E2 stack was blank in 2011 while LARGE E2 produced a 2011 value — spotted by the owner in the article figs. ROOT CAUSE (two independent research passes, primary statute verified verbatim by both): the workbook modelled the German BesAR from 2012 using the EEG 2012 tranche ladder, and had no BesAR treatment at all before that. Both are wrong. (1) REGIME DATING. The EEG 2012 §41(3) ladder (≤1 GWh full / 1–10 GWh 10% / 10–100 GWh 1% / >100 GWh 0.05 ct) FIRST APPLIES TO BENEFIT YEAR 2013, not 2012: §43(1) makes applications due 30 June effective 1 January of the FOLLOWING year, and §66(13) EEG 2012 applies §41 to applications made IN 2012. Benefit year 2012 rests on applications filed 30.06.2011, decided 16.12.2011 under EEG 2009. Empirical confirmation: privileged undertakings 734 (2012) → 1,691 (2013), Abnahmestellen 979 → 2,262, when the 1 GWh threshold bit. (2) THE 2010–2012 REGIME. EEG 2009 §§40–44 (Stammfassung, unamended to 31.12.2011) + §6 Abs.1 Nr.1 AusglMechV: NO tranches. A flat 0.05 ct/kWh on the privileged volume, plus a 10% SELBSTBEHALT charged at the full Umlage, disapplied only where the site clears BOTH ≥100 GWh AND ≥20% Stromkosten/Bruttowertschöpfung (§41(3) S.1 — "oder", so failing either limb keeps the Selbstbehalt). Eligibility >10 GWh and >15% BWS plus certification. Effective rate is therefore SCALE-INVARIANT for every teilbegünstigt site: 0.1×U + 0.9×0.05 ct. column2: EII eligibility definitions UK vs DE — and whether an eligibility-based output index is buildable
column3: Established while checking whether an output index could be built on the relief-eligibility lists (owner question 2026-07-24 about which index matches which archetype). UK: 71 four-digit NACE classes (SI 2015/721 Schedule) PLUS a hard firm-level test — electricity cost impact >= 20% of gross value added over three years (reg 8). GERMANY: 116 four-digit WZ classes (EnFG Anlage 2 = CEEAG Annex 1 verbatim) and NO intensity test at all — §30 requires only >1 GWh at the Abnahmestelle, an energy management system, and an efficiency/decarbonisation condition. The BesAR 14%/20% thresholds were abolished in the move to CEEAG. CONSEQUENCE FOR D67/D68: German eligibility is far easier to clear than British, so the German relieved population is much more fully populated within its sectors. This is INDEPENDENT CORROBORATION, from statute rather than from price data, of the population-matching reading — DE Eurostat band relief-dominated (implied relieved share 50-80% in the BesAR era) versus UK QEP band unrelieved-dominated (exempt ~15%). Two register corrections: the UK eligible-sector list lives in SI 2015/721, not SI 2024/409 (which only cross-refers); and Germany has no electricity-intensity test under EnFG. ALSO ESTABLISHED — an eligibility-based output index is NOT constructible symmetrically. ONS publishes the Index of Production at 3-digit at finest (96 industry labels, ZERO 4-digit CVM series) and five UK-eligible codes sit inside divisions 25-28 with no usable proxy; the one clean match is chemicals, where ONS 20A+20B is exactly the seven eligible division-20 classes. Germany is fully matchable (GENESIS 42153-0003, 195 four-digit series, 116/116 EnFG codes resolve). So the middle-tier output exhibit must remain the DIVISION-level energy-intensity definition (17/19/20/23/24) — which is what stage5 sections H/J already build and what Destatis itself publishes as "Energieintensive Industriezweige" (S196). column2: PROCUREMENT VINTAGE largely explains the 2024-25 UK observed-vs-modelled gap — and the sign flips in 2021/2023 rule out a purely definitional (QEP-basis) explanation. Demotes the Q92 gate.
column3: OWNER HYPOTHESIS 2026-07-25: "the difference between observed and modelled for UK in 2024 and 2025 is massive. I wonder if this is because industry got locked into very expensive contracts in 2023 ... the other being low uptake of exemptions." TESTED, and largely supported — with one date correction and one identification caveat. METHOD: back out the wholesale price IMPLIED by the observed bill = QEP (excl CCL) less every non-wholesale modelled component less the measured supply block, then compare it with the price the model assumes and with the forward curve (timeseries r113-118, diagnostic rows only — nothing downstream reads them). RESULT 1 — THE PLATEAU. UK LARGE implied wholesale: 2022 125.5 | 2023 130.3 | 2024 132.1 | 2025 132.4 GBP/MWh. Flat to within 7 GBP across four years while DAY-AHEAD went 211.8 -> 97.3 -> 75.7 -> 83.9 and the modelled front-year went 89.5 -> 273.7 -> 127.5 -> 79.7. UK MEDIUM plateaus higher: 166.5 / 165.2 / 154.6 for 2023-25. A four-year flat spot in a violently moving market is the smoothing signature of a laddered or multi-year-fixed book, not of a mis-specified stack. RESULT 2 — THE SIGN FLIPS ARE THE REAL EVIDENCE. Gap to E1 (excl CCL, nominal GBP/MWh), large: 2021 -46.6, 2022 +51.1, 2023 -122.2, 2024 +18.0, 2025 +59.5. A hedge protects on the way up and penalises on the way down, which is exactly this pattern. NOTHING DEFINITIONAL PRODUCES A -122 YEAR. This materially DEMOTES Q92 hypothesis (a) — that QEP is total spend per MWh and therefore structurally broader than a published-tariff build. Breadth of that kind is a level effect and would have to be positive in every year; it is not. Q92's gate should be re-scoped accordingly: still worth reading the QEP methodology note, but it is no longer the leading candidate. RESULT 3 — GERMANY IS A CLEAN CONTROL. DE LARGE implied wholesale: 2022 97.2 | 2023 107.8 | 2024 78.8 | 2025 65.4 EUR/MWh — it UNWINDS, and by 2025 sits BELOW the modelled front-year (88.7). Britain's sits 66% ABOVE its own (132.4 vs 79.7). Same crisis, same broad forward curves, opposite persistence. (DE levels are not comparable in absolute terms — the DE E1 stack is a relieved-band construct with a negative wedge, per D68 — but the SHAPE is.) DECOMPOSITION 2025, nominal GBP/MWh excl CCL, against the UNRELIEVED stack. LARGE: gap 59.5 = supply block + FiT (2025/26 unpublished) 7.0 + calm-year profile/shape/imbalance baseline 10.3 + PROCUREMENT VINTAGE ~29-33. MEDIUM: gap 81.7 = supply block + 7.0 + baseline 1.4 + PROCUREMENT VINTAGE ~60-64. THE RANGE IS THE 2025 SUPPLY-BLOCK IMPUTATION, which is not a measured number in 2025: holding the 2024 CSS reading (13.3) gives the low end, the 2012-24 nominal mean (9.0, the convention in diagnostic row r113) the high end, the article's real-terms period average (10.85) the middle. Quote ~30 (large) and ~62 (medium) and say it is bracketed, not measured. 2024 LARGE: gap only 18.0 and procurement vintage is -5.7, i.e. ESSENTIALLY CLOSED — because the model's own front-year price for delivery 2024 (127.45, struck in 2023) already sat near what industry actually paid. 2024 MEDIUM: gap 51.1, vintage +36.4. So the 'massive 2024 gap' is a MEDIUM-archetype phenomenon; at large size 2024 is unremarkable and only 2025 is extreme. OWNER DATE CORRECTION: the expensive lock-in year was 2022, not 2023. Front-year prices averaged 273.71 GBP/MWh through 2022 (for 2023 delivery) against 127.45 through 2023. Contracts SIGNED IN 2022 covering 2023-25 delivery are the costly ones. ON THE SECOND MECHANISM: relief take-up is real but acts on a DIFFERENT part of the gap. By construction it cannot explain anything above E1 — E1 already assumes no relief. It explains the E1-to-E2 span (79 USD/MWh large in 2025), i.e. about 59% of the total observed-to-relieved gap. Both of the owner's mechanisms are live; they are not competing. IDENTIFICATION CAVEAT — STATE THIS WHENEVER THE NUMBER IS USED: 'procurement vintage' is a LABELLED RESIDUAL, not a measurement. Any unmodelled cost that grew after 2022 lands in the same bucket. What licenses the label is the plateau, the sign flips and the German control, not the arithmetic itself. FALSIFIABLE PREDICTION (the honest test): a hedge legacy MUST unwind. The modelled 2026 wholesale is 81.21 GBP/MWh. If the 2026 and 2027 QEP prints fall toward it, this is confirmed; if the implied series plateaus at ~130 for a fifth and sixth year, it is NOT hedging and something structural is being missed. Diarise against the QEP quarterly releases. || UPDATE 2026-07-26 (S204): (a) METHODOLOGY CONFIRMED — the DESNZ industrial-price methodology note states the QEP band price is total value / total volume across ALL sales the surveyed suppliers make in the quarter (PT survey, 6 electricity suppliers, ~60% coverage, bands per EU 2016/1952): an average over every contract in force, NOT new contracts — exactly the averaging a vintage story requires. (b) FIRST OUT-OF-SAMPLE PRINT — QEP June-2026 (Q1-2026, provisional): XL 20.973 p/kWh, Large 23.366. Q1-on-Q1 implied wholesale (each year's annual components): LARGE 143.5 (Q1-25) -> 121.9 (Q1-26) GBP/MWh, -15%; MEDIUM 168.3 -> 139.3, -17%; front-year flat 79.7 -> 81.2. Excess over front-year: large 63.8 -> 40.7 (-36%), medium 88.6 -> 58.1 (-34%). FIRST decline since the plateau began — direction and pace consistent with 2022-vintage contracts rolling off. NOT yet confirmation: full-year 2026/2027 prints must continue toward 81.21; Q1 figures are provisional (finalised +3 months). Exhibit: out-of-sample panel added to procurement_vintage.html.

column2: GAS-SRMC IDENTITY TEST: British wholesale power IS gas marginal cost to within a few pounds in every non-crisis year; Germany only as a ceiling; China is a coal-anchor, not a market margin
column3: OWNER HYPOTHESIS 2026-07-25: high 2020s wholesale is gas, 'since it's the marginal producer'; proposed an LCOE chart. ANALYST RESPONSE: LCOE answers entry/anchor economics, not hourly price formation — the right test is the marginal-cost identity. BUILT: SRMC = (hub gas HHV + carbon x 0.18296 tCO2/MWh_th)/efficiency, central 50% HHV, corridor 46% (~NESO 0.394 intensity convention) to 55% (H-class). Inputs S198 (gas: Ofgem/ONS-SAP/BNetzA/EC/ACER primaries, EI SR 2025 bridge for UK 2010-13+2017 and TTF 2010-20, estimated=Y) and S199 (carbon cross-checks; prices themselves from the workbook's own carbon!r13/r5 series for house consistency). Diagnostic rows timeseries r119-125; nothing downstream reads them. RESULT UK — THE IDENTITY HOLDS: DA minus SRMC50, calm years (excl 2021-22), mean +3.7 GBP/MWh, SD 3.5; 2013 +1.4, 2023 +2.4, 2024 -1.8, 2025 -0.8. The only material excursions: 2016 +10.6 (French nuclear outage autumn) and the crisis years +24/+35 (scarcity + within-year shape at annual granularity). Gas does not merely set the British price often — at annual resolution there is essentially NOTHING in the British wholesale price except gas fuel cost and carbon. Carbon is not a minor term: the UK applicable price (UKA/EUA + CPS) contributes ~24-27% of SRMC in 2023-25 (2025: 11.96 of 84.7) and the CPS wedge is why UK carbon cost exceeded the German from 2013 to ~2020. RESULT DE — GAS IS A CEILING, NOT THE PRICE: DA minus SRMC50 runs -8.5 mean 2012-18 (hard coal/lignite at the margin; gas SRMC was NOT the German price), ~0 in 2019-21 (fuel-switch era), -13.9 mean 2023-25 (gas sets a shrinking share of hours; renewables/coal displace it). SO: the UK-DE observed wholesale difference is a MERIT-ORDER difference, not a hub-price difference — NBP and TTF track each other. RESULT CN: no marginal-pricing market at all (catalogue/benchmark +-20% band anchored on coal); the China gap is a FUEL-ANCHOR difference — coal LCOE ~$65-67 (lcoe r21) + regulated formation + zero carbon (carbon tab A2). LCOE'S PROPER ROLE (owner's chart, correctly placed): the anchor comparison — CN coal $67 / CN CCGT $103 vs UK CCGT $186 (DESNZ EGC 2023, incl fuel+carbon at DESNZ assumptions) and DE GuD $121-201 (Fraunhofer ISE 2024) — and the 'LCOE does not bid' point: UK onshore wind $62 / solar $67 LCOE do not lower the hourly price while gas is marginal; they lower COSTS via CfDs/PPAs (a levy-side story the article already tells) and volumes, not the marginal price. CAVEATS: annual-average identity, not hourly stack modelling — no capture of within- year shape (visible 2021-22); UK gas 2010-13/2017 and TTF 2010-20 are EI-SR-derived (secondary, flagged); efficiency convention spans 46-55%, central 50% chosen a priori not fitted; SRMC starts 2013 UK / 2012 DE where the workbook carbon series start (ICAP 2010-11 EUA in S199 if ever needed). EXHIBIT: wholesale_anatomy.html (artifact wholesale-anatomy). Staging: gas_srmc_staging.md.

column2: GAS RENT LEDGER: UKCS extraction is CHEAP by world standards — the bill question is who collects the price-minus-cost wedge; nationalise-at-cost ceiling ~3.5bn/yr, largely funded by cancelling the Exchequer take, duration-capped by an 18-month gas inventory
column3: OWNER QUESTIONS 2026-07-25: international unit-operating-cost comparison; 'would increasing E&P spending and perhaps even nationalising the companies extracting gas materially lower the cost of gas for the UK?'; owner hypothesis that UK extraction costs are high but domestic gas avoids liquefaction/transport. FINDINGS: (1) LIKE-FOR-LIKE UOC COMPARISON IS NOT CONSTRUCTABLE (already documented r22): NSTA UOC is mixed oil+gas; other jurisdictions publish on different bases. The constructable comparison is DELIVERED COST BY ROUTE (r47, OIES-based): UK domestic <$5/MMBtu, Norway pipe <$6, Qatar LNG ~$5-6, US LNG full-cycle ~$8.5-9 at 2025 HH — against a 2025 market price ~$12 (TTF; NBP within ~$0.5). SO: UK extraction is NOT expensive by world standards; the owner's liquefaction intuition is CORRECT (~$4-5/MMBtu avoided vs a US cargo) but under market pricing that saving accrues as PRODUCER RENT, not a consumer discount — Norway is the proof (cheapest producer in Europe, consumers pay market, rent goes to the fund). (2) MORE E&P SPENDING does not move the consumer price (price-taker, 3.5% of traded gas, section 9); cheaper extraction just widens the rent. (3) NATIONALISE-AND-SELL-AT-COST is a RENT TRANSFER, not a cost reduction. Ledger 2025 (r45): price 30.40 GBP/MWh, full-cycle cost proxy 20.29 (MIXED basis, flagged), wedge 10.11; at the 78% marginal rate the wedge splits Exchequer 7.89 / producer 2.22. CEILING (r46): 10.11 x 344 TWh = ~3.5bn GBP/yr = ~5 GBP/MWh across all gas consumed — vs HMRC actual take 4.47bn FY2024-25 (all UKCS incl oil) and OBR 2.7bn forecast 2025-26: the scheme is largely a transfer FROM the Exchequer, i.e. from taxpayers to gas users. DURATION: proven gas inventory ~1,020 TWh = 18 months of consumption / 3 years of production; the scheme's sustainability depends on the E&P investment whose returns it confiscates (and capex already collapsed 22bn->6bn real, r42). ELECTRICITY VARIANT: directing at-cost gas to power stations would cut power SRMC materially (gas at 12 vs 30 -> SRMC ~36 GBP/MWh) but is the same transfer at larger scale — a Strompreisbremse funded by foregone tax, eroding with the inventory. CAVEATS: cost proxy is mixed oil+gas (no gas-only exists — NG-148); 78% is marginal not average (allowances/decom relief); delivered-cost bases heterogeneous (2021 real-2022$ marginal-field stacks vs 2025 build-ups); NBP~TTF approx unsourced. Article: section 9 extension + fig12 (two panels). S202.
column5: RESOLVED as a finding 2026-07-25. Owner-directed exhibit (market-vs-nationalised split bars) drawn as fig12 right panel. Re-run pieces: HMRC stats each Sept; OBR EFO; OIES updates; OGPM regime from 2030.

column2: UKCS RESOURCE LADDER & FINDING CURVE: 2C discovered-but-unsanctioned (6.2 bn boe) is >3x proven; the exploration yield is stable (50% success, GBP 2-4/boe) — the INPUT collapsed; sanctioning, not geology, binds at the 2030 horizon
column3: OWNER QUESTION 2026-07-25: 'data on potential reserves if E&P were increased? Or can we construct new reserves vs E&P spending?' BOTH constructable (r48-51, S203). (1) LADDER end-2024: 1P 1.9 / 2P 2.9 / 2C 6.2 bn boe (gas 2.0 = ~3,400 TWh = FIVE years of UK consumption, on top of 1.5 yrs in 1P) / mapped prospective 4.6 risked mean / 11.2 play-level. The discovered-but-unsanctioned stock is >3x the proven stock; 2.0 bn boe of it sits on UNLICENSED acreage; only 0.3 bn boe of prospects are drill-ready. (2) FINDING CURVE: yield is documented and STABLE - ~50% exploration success over two decades, historic finding cost GBP 2-4/boe; what collapsed is input: E&A origin wells 49 (2010) -> 7 (2024; 3 expl = 10-yr low), E&A capex 1.4bn -> 0.1-0.2bn, discoveries 239/240/212 mmboe (2018-20) -> <=100/yr (2021-24) vs production 401 -> replacement ratio -14% in 2024, and in 2024 exactly TWO consents moved <50 mmboe from 2C to reserves. At the OGA KPI-era rate (200 mmboe/yr on ~1-1.5bn E&A) exploration replaces roughly a third to half of gas production - the bigger near-term lever is SANCTIONING the existing 2C. (3) SCENARIOS: Westwood/OEUK low 2.57 vs high 4.26 bn boe to 2050 (delta 1.69 bn boe ~ 2,870 TWh-e over 25 yrs); NSTA central halves output again by 2030; discovery->production ~5 yrs. (4) STUDY IMPLICATION: none of this touches the PRICE (Q95 price-taker); it moves import share (OEUK: LNG 14% -> >25% by 2030 no-action vs 6% with support), the current account, and the DURATION of the Q95 rent arithmetic - sanctioning the 2C gas stretches the nationalise-at-cost runway from ~18 months toward 5+ years of consumption, at the cost of the 'substantial investment' (NSTA) whose returns the 78% regime and any confiscation debate govern. CAVEATS: wells series is OWN TABULATION from NSTA open data (published anchors agree within definitional variance); 2021/23/24 discoveries are <= bounds; 2C viability heterogeneous (marginal/unlicensed dominated); prospective volumes risked but pre-drill; Westwood/OEUK is an industry-commissioned scenario set. Article: section 9 extension + fig13.
column5: RESOLVED as a finding 2026-07-25. Re-run on each NSTA R&R edition (~Oct) and Wells Insights (~Oct/Nov); watch the Jackdaw/Rosebank reserves reclassification.

column2: CCL RELIEF IS MEASURABLE AND WAS UNDER-MODELLED: min/met processes are fully exempt (2014+), and the QEP 3.4.2-minus-3.4.1 difference publishes how much CCL the band actually pays — 58% of the main rate in 2025, as low as 19% in 2010
column3: TRIGGER 2026-07-26: owner asked why the observed line excludes CCL, then whether firms can be exempted from it. FINDINGS. (1) TWO RELIEF ROUTES, only one of which the build knew about. The CCA reduced rate (electricity discount 92% from 01.04.2023 through 01.04.2027 per gov.uk CCL rates) was known and deliberately not modelled (D29: 'no privileged rate publishable'). The FULL EXEMPTION for mineralogical and metallurgical processes (HMRC Notice CCL1/3 s3.14 + Annex A, in force 01.04.2014, ~30 listed processes: cement, lime, flat glass, ceramics / steel, aluminium and other metal processing; covers ELECTRICITY, not just fuels) was NOT in the workbook at all — no mention anywhere before today. Electrolytic processes (chlor-alkali; hydrogen from 12.03.2026) are non-fuel use and also outside the levy. THREE of the study's FOUR output-index commodities (steel, aluminium, cement) sit inside the exemption; paper does not. (2) THE RELIEF IS MEASURED, NOT UNMEASURABLE. DESNZ publishes the same bands both ways; 3.4.2 minus 3.4.1 = CCL actually borne by the band. Extra Large band, CCL paid as % of statutory main rate: 2010 19.4 / 2012 27.7 / 2015 33.8 / 2018 51.7 / 2020 80.6 / 2021 91.0 / 2022 87.5 / 2023 51.6 / 2024 57.9 / 2025 58.4. The 2010-14 level (~20-25%) is consistent with near-universal CCA coverage at the then-80% discount; the climb to 91% by 2021 implies relief coverage FELL sharply across the decade; the 2022->2023 drop (87.5 -> 51.6) is unexplained and worth a look. CAVEAT: derived as the difference of two published series whose band composition shifts year to year — read the level and the direction, not single-year moves. Banked timeseries r132-134 (diagnostic; nothing downstream reads them). (3) CONSEQUENCE FOR THE MODEL — see D71. E2 carried the full main rate; correct figure for a min/met EII is zero. E2 overstated by ~10 USD/MWh 2024-25 (the CCL was the ENTIRE residual levy in the exempt case — E2 levies now compute to exactly 0.00 in 2024 and 2025, confirming the article's own 'the residual is mainly the CCL'). Section-5 convergence inverts: relieved UK large now ~9 USD/MWh BELOW Germany. (4) OWN-ERROR NOTE. The excl-CCL observed basis was defended on the ground that the incl-CCL series would embed unmeasurable CCA relief. That reasoning was repeated to the owner before it was tested; it is wrong twice over — the relief is published (2), and the excl-CCL choice created a worse asymmetry, pairing an excl-tax UK observed line with an incl-tax UK stack and an incl-tax German observed line. OPEN: the 2022->2023 effective-rate drop; whether any archetype-level split (min/met vs paper) is worth modelling separately; CCA scheme successor arrangements beyond the current targets.
